# Uniform exponent-1/2 continuation

The target remains unproved: for every fixed `C > 0`, bound the number of
lattice points on every centered-circle arc of length `C sqrt(R)` by a
constant depending only on `C`. No uniform exceptional-set theorem has been
assumed, and no endpoint theorem has been added as an axiom.

Research priority: improve the dependence on `R`, ultimately to a constant.
Leading-constant improvements and near-saturation classifications are
secondary; they do not handle hypothetical unbounded families with
`M=o(log R/log log R)` and are not the current research objective.

The strongest current general **prose** estimate is now
`M <= (1+epsilon) log R/log log R` for fixed `C,epsilon>0` and
sufficiently large `R`; see item 30. It is uniform in arc position
but still grows with the radius. The Lean-verified asymptotic
theorem retains leading constant `8+epsilon`. Neither establishes
the requested radius-independent bound.

The current [Claude handoff](claude_handoff_uniform_endpoint.md) gives
the exact target, independent-review priorities, alternative unrestricted
formulations, and the distinction between checked results and unfinished
ideas. Item 532 below proves a stronger exact extraction with nested prime
overlap and aggregate logarithmic residual height `O(W/M)`. A new height
lower bound is still needed; the general growth rate is unchanged.

Item 533 gives a new geometric obstruction in the polynomial model:
constant-imaginary, equal-degree full Boolean blocks have at most 35
nonanchor rows, independently of degree. Repeated roots are allowed,
but distinct blocks and their conjugates must be coprime. A double
Kummer cover and Bogomolov--Miyaoka--Yau prove the bound. No transfer
from arbitrary integer profiles to these polynomial families is known.

Item 499 closes the algebraic-offset escape for fixed Pisot norm paths
in a cubic field of signature `(1,1)`. A Subspace Theorem gcd estimate
retains the primitive radius, and a finite-contact argument handles
rational limiting phases. Every correction producing an endpoint pair
has height greater than `T^kappa`, eventually, for each `kappa<1/6`.
This theorem is uniform in the path index, not in the field or profile.

At the user's request, item 500 imports and extends the random-conjugation
rectangle argument from the Gaussian-prime paper in `openai/math`.
It applies to prime-disjoint composite Gaussian blocks. The actual
endpoint chords still meet a critical determinant threshold, and the
source's cheap shared-displacement entropy hypothesis fails on a short
circle arc. The general point-count growth remains unchanged.

Item 501 strengthens the rectangle method to a deterministic forbidden
interval for two signed products to have short witnesses. Applied to a
fixed extracted row, it excludes every change of fewer than half of its
incident block orientations at the same near-real height. Item 502 gives
an unbounded, exact gap between ordinary divisor compatibility and the
Gaussian least radius. Neither supplies the missing height gap for the
whole configuration; the uniform objective remains unproved.

Items 503--504 test the remaining signed-witness and state-update routes.
Every proper raw block flip has large imaginary height when its original
multiplier is retained, but an exact disjoint-block Pell family shows
that a constant complex multiplier can repair a half flip. Relations
among two or three distinct raw signed products require a large
coefficient. The Pell family realizes a four-term circuit with two
changing groups and bounded coefficients; item 505 supplies a family
with three large changing groups as well.
Multiplicative phase updates do preserve residues exactly, but make the
Gaussian-moat zero-avoidance test uninformative on a fixed norm fiber.
These conclusions do not improve the general growth rate.

Items 505--507 separate algebraic signed circuits from actual thin
witnesses. Two independent circuits obey a coefficient-height product
bound, whereas a single bounded-coefficient circuit can have three
large groups. Conjugation sharpens the witness interval to leave only
half-distance or antipodal pairs on one fixed balanced support.
Most substantially, four corrected witnesses in the common-support
pattern `DABC,DA bar(B)bar(C),D bar(A)B bar(C),D bar(A)bar(B)C`
satisfy `min(N(A),N(B),N(C))<=8 M^2 max(1,Y)^4`, without any balance
assumption. Here `M` is the largest correction modulus and `Y` the
largest imaginary coordinate. This gives a positive height exponent
for that pattern. The missing step is to construct it from the
different supports of the actual circle rows; the general growth
bound and the unproved status of the uniform goal are unchanged.

Items 508--510 extend the signed-witness argument to all eight
four-word pattern groups and identify the multiplicative words
that fit the endpoint height budget. The actual four-row pair
quotients admit exact small-determinant triangle frames and an
additive gcd recovering each row's two private norm groups.
However, loop traces depend only on the small residuals, and a
primitive Pell cycle survives the simplest additive test. These
results still give no height gap for the full Boolean profile.

Items 511--513 settle further Pell tests. An explicit primitive
eight-point family realizes the translated Hadamard pattern on
endpoint arcs, showing why the origin-based gap cannot be applied
there without additional information. It attains the existing
fixed-template bound of eight. That count bound now also covers
every fixed real-quadratic norm-one Pell unit: a possible higher-order
phase cancellation is excluded by its coefficient cost and Gaussian
prefactor parity. Norm-minus-one units allow more cancellation, but
still give at most 4096 rows in the stated asymptotic template model.
These are uniform counts within fixed templates; the general bound
in `R` has not improved.

Items 514--516 continue the source-inspired factorization route.
An actual-coordinate gcd recovers each co-singleton core norm and
selects at most one nearest-square sign in the endpoint regime.
For arbitrary fixed affine Fibonacci rates, exact cyclotomic layers
now account for every growing Gaussian overlap before measuring the
primitive radius. Within one proportional class, the endpoint problem
becomes a reciprocal cyclotomic-polynomial fiber, with a converse
realization. Such a family has at most four rows if its active layer
indices are odd prime powers, and at most 128 if each has at most
two distinct prime divisors. All profiles through polynomial degree
40 have also been checked exhaustively and have at most four rows.
Those restricted counts are superseded within the one-class model by
items 518--521 below. They do not improve the general dependence on `R`.

Items 517--522 now prove a uniform bound for the **entire one-class
cyclotomic model**: at most 2251 rows, with arbitrary odd indices,
prime powers and multiplicities. The proof uses an affine embedding,
a prime-power compression preserving nullity, and a roots-of-unity
intersection graph. An exact five-row family with normalized arc length
tending to zero also disproves the earlier proposed four-row count.
Mixed affine classes have coupled low-frequency equations; a large
rational kernel need not contain even one admissible bounded integer
difference. Arbitrary circle configurations have not been reduced to
this model. The general uniform goal remains unproved.

Items 523--524 now handle bounded integer differences in mixed classes.
With a common slope, large harmonics separate by algebraic conjugation;
three-prime Ramanujan congruences recover every missing small harmonic.
Colored compression then bounds the actual row affine dimension. This
gives an absolute count with arbitrary intercepts and odd layers, even
though the full rational coupled kernel can still have unbounded dimension.
The argument also covers arbitrarily many distinct slope values when
their 2-adic valuations are distinct. Item 526 now handles further
families with overlapping frequencies; general incomparable slope sets
and the transfer to arbitrary circle configurations remain unresolved.

Items 525--527 add an exact compression extension, a broader uniform
template count, and a full-profile arithmetic filter. Compression works
for any selected set of Möbius rows, though it need not preserve omitted
row values. Integral packet projections now give the same absolute
count `8589936843` when the slopes in each 2-adic valuation bucket form
a divisibility chain, or when each bucket has at most two arbitrary
slopes. The proof preserves low phase coefficients in each original
class and charges the kernel of the composed map only once. Separately,
the actual residuals satisfy an exact imaginary-content gcd identity,
but dividing out that content generally destroys the row norms and
Gaussian block divisibilities. These results do not change the general
growth bound in `R`; the full uniform circle theorem remains unproved.

Items 528--530 extend the count to further incomparable slope families
and test two more possible bridges. The same uniform template bound
now holds when each 2-adic slope bucket has at most three original
affine classes, including one class at each of slopes `6,10,14`.
This is not a bound for three slope groups containing arbitrarily
many classes. A simultaneous multiprime packet split preserves low
jets with a factor-three cost, but exact examples rule out general
cost preservation or a uniform cost factor for complete base refinement.
A positive integer Hankel determinant has exact Boolean core divisors;
their guaranteed exponents fall below its size at every proper minor
and are only critical at the top. These advances and barriers do not
prove the general mixed-template count or the uniform circle theorem.

Item 497 proves a positive correction-height cost for one norm-descent
mechanism. A fixed Gaussian root and a constant imaginary polynomial norm
force `X(c)/Y` to be irrational at every rational parameter `c`.
Along a Pisot-unit path tending to such a parameter at the contracting
embeddings, the descended phase has a fixed irrational algebraic limit.
Rational rotations that turn it into an endpoint pair require height
`T^[delta/(D(2D+1))]`, even after arbitrary common Gaussian content is
removed. In the explicit pure cubic example this is `epsilon^(n/42)`.
This is a restricted descent obstruction, not the residual-height gap
needed for arbitrary profiles. The general point-count growth is unchanged.
Item 498 shows that the rational-offset assumption matters: an explicit
degree-16 row has a rational limiting phase at an algebraic offset, while
retaining all the single-row norm hypotheses. No endpoint configuration
or linear splitting follows from that example.

Items 493--494 separate the remaining cubic norm condition from the
full root-incidence problem. Every real cubic field admits an explicit
monic quartic with the fixed root `i` and constant imaginary norm, so
neither total reality nor the single-row trace condition excludes descent.
For degree-eight rows that do split in the coefficient field, the common
rational factor and allowable Galois-orbit collisions are constrained.
These conditions have not excluded a full four-row profile.

Items 495--496 close the linear-splitting question for one explicit cyclic
cubic quartic family: a fixed prime excludes every rational parameter,
including parameters with arbitrary positive or negative valuation.
Polynomial composition cannot repair this failure of splitting.
The complete quartic classification has a second parameter, a rational
basis rotation. The obstruction covers every such rotation for unit
parameters at 17, but a proved local splitting family shows why the
same prime cannot settle every case. None of these results improves
the general point-count growth bound.

Items 490--492 give arithmetic restrictions on descending an algebraic
polynomial profile by field norms. A fixed Gaussian root excludes every
even-degree descent that preserves constant imaginary parts. An exact
content calculation for the five actual circle points retains all
resultant-prime depths. The quadratic case admits a stronger exclusion:
a full profile with three or more rows cannot keep every descended
imaginary degree within the endpoint threshold when the primitive
content is bounded. The certified profile's coefficient field is still
unknown, and these results do not give a general point-count improvement.

Items 487--489 repair prime-power bookkeeping in the integer star lift,
prove a four-row nearest-square Gram rigidity criterion, and audit exactly
which hypothetical residual-height bounds would improve growth. Four
simultaneously small norm defects force an integral near-axis realization;
the missing step is to exclude those defects or force residual growth.
An exact three-column Pell family shows why the fourth column is necessary
for this general rank argument. No arithmetic height gap or stronger
general point-count bound is claimed.

Items 482--486 reduce the four-row integer smallness condition to one
nearest-square remainder and three Gaussian divisibilities, and expose
an exact five-vertex symmetry in the polynomial system. Five star
quintics have real span at most four; the certified solution has span
exactly four and admits a common degree-four/degree-three frame applied
to affine pairs. Rationality imposes simultaneous negative-square
discriminants and a common Gaussian norm class. These conditions retain
the contact requirements and do not yet exclude integer profiles.
Eight contacts now uniquely reconstruct a genuine frame; rational input
would force the frame and private roots to be rational. An exact integer
five-star lift retains all correction factors, but its generic relation
lattice still gives no arithmetic height gap. A separate moment invariant
excludes every common real-quadratic extension of the certified four-row
profile and of the entire known vertical three-row family, including
their reanchorings. Arbitrary larger profiles need not arise by such
extensions. The general growth estimate is unchanged.

Items 476--481 extend the three-row construction to a rational family
and prove a general polynomial-to-integer specialization theorem. Every
fixed polynomial profile of the required kind yields actual primitive,
prime-disjoint integer profiles and short arcs. Profiles in arbitrarily
large row counts would contradict uniformity, but existence is currently
established only for two and three rows. The new pairwise Vieta criterion
retains correction primes and shows that the known three-row family has
no integral pair alternate. A necessary six-pair polynomial identity has
a coprime positive norm solution, so that isolated condition cannot
exclude four rows. A direct four-row search then produced a candidate
whose existence is now certified by exact rational contraction bounds:
the full fifteen-block real polynomial system is nondegenerately
solvable. Its coefficients are real algebraic, with rationality still
unproved, so the integer specialization theorem does not yet apply.
No growth improvement or uniform bound follows.

Items 471--475 audit the extraction in growing dimension and construct
an actual unbounded three-row full Boolean family. Its seven blocks
are balanced and prime-disjoint, its rows are conjugate-primitive, and
its imaginary coordinates and determinant residuals are fixed constants.
It gives four lattice points on arcs of order `R^(3/7)`, a fixed point
count rather than a failure of uniformity. A universal residual-height
exclusion in this formulation must therefore use at least four nonanchor
rows. The two-dimensional lattice and all-anchor radius audits do not
provide that exclusion. An explicit elliptic descent rules out quadratic
composition as one way to extend this particular family. The best general
point-count growth is unchanged.

Items 465--470 retain the exact norm equations and conjugate-primitivity
of the actual anchor numerators. The new moment system has a balanced
countermodel when separated from the metric equations. After all moment
compatibilities, one area equation suffices for Euclidean realization;
the integral lift is automatic when one prescribed norm is Gaussian.
All integral realizations of the fixed oriented Gram matrix differ only
in a common Gaussian factor of norm
`d=gcd({N_i},{Delta_ij})`. Under the full profile, `log d=w+o(w)`.
Primitive orientations and ordinary row contents can be repaired with
only subpower factor losses. Tiny imaginary coordinates select at most
one integral rotation of each fixed metric, but its existence has not
been excluded. The general growth estimate is unchanged.

Items 456--464 prove all-distinct localized generation, give its
Eagon--Northcott resolution, and control integral generation by
fixed powers of residual brackets and row contents, independently
of coalition depth. The full primitive family has index `exp(o(w))`
under the extracted profile. These results also isolate an invalid
proposed height comparison:
a large minor of a redundant generator matrix does not lower-bound
the lattice covolume. The new arithmetic generation results do not
yet produce a vector below the twelve-row coefficient threshold `90w`.
Generic determinant-coordinate divisibility has a sharp all-size cap
at the existing covolume budget, so that proposed improvement also
requires extra arithmetic information from the actual configurations.

Items 353--354 add nonlinear real-root ordering constraints and use them
to exclude all 21,120 odd-positive degree-22 deletions from one tensor
Hadamard construction. This resolves the moment feasibility left open by
the earlier certificate and variation tests for that family. It does not
reduce arbitrary endpoint configurations to fixed rational templates, so
the general growth estimate remains unchanged. Item 357 excludes every
punctured orthogonal eight-row template of length sixteen, and item 359
reduces the corresponding all-degree necessary conditions to a finite
weighted graph. Item 363 constructs exact weighted paths in infinitely
many degrees, so these conditions alone cannot give the proposed
all-degree exclusion. Actual real magnitudes remain an additional
requirement, and the Pell fixture in item 362 shows why endpoint
proximity does not automatically supply the moment hypotheses. Item 364
retains the unknown magnitudes in a full-row-space positivity condition,
with explicit Christoffel and Vandermonde consequences. Item 365 now
characterizes those scalar and determinant relaxations and constructs
magnitudes passing them on the admissible word family. The full moment
equations remain unresolved. Items 366--367 factor specific common-twist
determinants exactly into ordinary scalar character coordinates, retaining
all rational content but giving no new radius exponent.

Items 368--371 audit nonlinear angular compression and pair reflection
on actual Gaussian data. Explicit four-point families defeat two cubic
compression maps after their exact least radii are charged. A separate
coefficient bound remains valid for rational maps of growing degree,
including maps fixing selected source directions. The reflection bound
retains nested-prime cancellation and is sharp at the allocation-profile
level. These restrict proposed transformations; they do not improve the
general growth estimate or establish the uniform bound.

Items 372--376 weaken the sufficient intrinsic arithmetic target and
retain more of the simultaneous moment equations. A balanced bonus larger
than `2/5` suffices in the eight-row test; another sufficient target is
the source-gcd inequality `A^6 F^3<=exp(B)N`. Both remain unproved for
arbitrary endpoint tuples. The full template equations imply new coupled
three- and four-row product identities, while the previously constructed
Euler words now admit exact positive integer magnitudes satisfying the
first moment. Some exact words admit integer magnitudes satisfying both
that moment and all 36 quartet log-sign inequalities under the prescribed
spectral order. Their full moment Jacobians have generic full column rank,
but exceptional ordered nodes remain unresolved. Neither construction
supplies the higher odd moments or the connection from arbitrary endpoint
arcs to these templates.

Items 377--378 distinguish exact scalar values from signs and from the
full polynomial equations. A two-quartet tradeoff excludes the specific
magnitudes used in item 376. A new construction on the same word family
then satisfies the first moment and every scalar cross ratio with different
positive real magnitudes and auxiliary coefficients. Item 381 now proves
that these magnitudes cannot satisfy the full moments. Other magnitudes
on the same words remain unresolved. The best general growth estimate
is unchanged.

Items 379--380 give an exact source-exponent criterion for a common
quarter-root field and a different necessary condition for full moments.
The latter fixes reciprocal-sum order and makes a weighted cross Gram
matrix have rank exactly three, with explicit nonzero minors. The field
criterion alone has actual nonendpoint examples with uncontrolled
pair-layer mass. Neither result proves the required intrinsic inequality
or the uniform endpoint bound.

Items 381--383 apply and strengthen the reciprocal conditions. On the
published Euler-word family, every magnitude tuple from the prescribed
barycentric recipe fails the full moments, even before later columns are
shifted. This also excludes every tuple in item 378, regardless of its
shift sizes. The proof uses a critical pair's reciprocal identity, sign
order and the recipe's minimum spacing. Other positive magnitudes on
those words remain unresolved. Full moments also force an exact Hankel
projection identity on each cross support, with strict lower-degree
inequalities and positive quadrature identities. Fourth reciprocal
moments bound each support's effective reciprocal-square mass by an
absolute constant. These results do not improve the general dependence
on the circle radius.

Item 384 proves a limitation of the reciprocal relaxation itself. An
exact finite construction satisfies the orthogonal-code condition, common
first moment, all reciprocal cross Gram equations and the appropriate
within-group distance signs together. Every cross support nevertheless
fails the critical root order and fourth reciprocal coefficient equation.
Simultaneous higher moments, and a transfer from arbitrary endpoint arcs,
remain missing.

Items 385--386 retain more of the higher reciprocal equations. The
fourth-order cross Gram has an exact rank-one quotient and explicit
bordered minors. A separate compactness argument proves a uniform
reciprocal-square tail bound on every critical support, independent of
degree after normalizing its smallest magnitude. Thus its magnitude
count up to a factor `T` is uniformly `o(T^2)`. This concerns template
magnitudes, not circle radius or lattice-point count; the requested
uniform endpoint bound and the general growth estimate are unchanged.

Item 387 strengthens the exact-support tail theorem to explicit linear
magnitude growth and an `O(1/K)` reciprocal-square tail. It uses the real
intermediate polynomial fibers and a positive harmonic function on the
upper half-plane. Item 388 shows that Paley profiles can satisfy every
subset determinant test and the known pair and four-row phase tests while
requiring at least half their prime-cut mass to be exceptional in any
Walsh extraction. These profiles have no proved endpoint localization.
Neither result changes the general circle-point bound.

Items 389--390 delimit two analytic relaxations. The entire residual
identities allow arbitrarily many rows against one opposing row, without
finite orthogonality or the required balanced split. Finitely many exact
reciprocal coefficient identities also allow a positive mass of arbitrarily
small reciprocal roots, even with distinct absolute values. These are
explicit limitations of the proposed intermediate conditions, not
counterexamples to the uniform circle bound.

Items 391--393 settle the remaining individual character tests in an
unbounded Paley family. A skew-Hadamard argument gives the exact minimum
`B=bM/2-2` over all nonzero saturated characters for the canonical
assignment. A separate prime-field polynomial argument covers every
capacity-two assignment at sufficiently large prime orders and classifies
all norm-one ternary characters. Actual distinct nearby split primes
preserve the strict half-height excess uniformly in character amplitude.
These same profiles can pass all subset determinant tests while refusing
the proposed Walsh extraction. Their actual source phases are still
uncontrolled. Joint angular constraints or a different arithmetic input
are required; the general growth estimate remains unchanged.

Item 394 sharpens this diagnosis. Complex factors with actual split-prime
squared moduli can have compatible endpoint phases while every nonzero
saturated character satisfies both Gaussian coordinate lower bounds.
This holds at `W=20M log M+O_C(M)`, using a convergent countable union
bound. The factors and rows are not Gaussian integers. Thus phase
compatibility and these coordinate gaps together still leave joint
integrality missing. Item 395 identifies the generators of linear
common-axis elimination with scalar difference characters and gives an
actual Gaussian family with only one scale of determinant-gcd height.
Nonlinear combinations and special evaluated divisibility remain open.

Items 396--398 return to actual ordered lattice points. The exact index
of consecutive affine circuits retains the content lost by multiplying
their primitive coefficients. At five points it charges every prime
layer separating the two extreme rows from the three interior rows,
including nested allocations and accidental triangle content. An
unproved bound on the conductor-supported part of this index with any
fixed exponent below `1/15` would imply the full uniform theorem.
The elementary exponent is still `1/4`, so this is a sufficient arithmetic
reduction, not an improvement to the general circle-count growth rate.
An ordered-average application of the existing obtuse Bessel theorem
also controls arbitrary fixed local tests without exchangeability.

Items 399--401 refine this target and explain a restricted family.
Only the reduced denominator of the outer-pair/interior-triple primitive
squared-radius product needs control; accidental contributions to the
affine index are unnecessary and can be locally arbitrarily large.
A complete six-column code classification proves that every admissible
five-row equal-sum family avoids the extreme-pair source cut in cubic
phase order. This bounds the forced denominator for fixed six-factor
Gaussian families by their norm-collision resultants. Neither the fixed
coefficients nor the exact first-moment condition have been extracted
from arbitrary endpoint arcs, so the general growth estimate is unchanged.
The same classification also transports the existing primitive-content
theorem to give a coefficient-uniform normalized arc lower bound
`1/sqrt(10)` for the specified signed six-factor equal-sum products,
including moving rational parameters. It retains their row-sign convention
and does not cover arbitrary independent units or approximate moments.

Items 402--407 test the next symmetry steps. An exact rational contraction
certificate gives a real ten-factor critical-moment solution with an
extreme-pair source column in its actual eventual phase order. Thus the
six-factor cut exclusion does not extend using those real moment
conditions alone; rational coefficients and Gaussian integrality remain
separate requirements. The forced factor `K` also has an exact oriented
descent: dividing the outer pair and interior triple by conjugate factors
produces a primitive tuple of norm `N/K`. This separates the two angular
clusters, so it does not yet give an induction retaining one short arc.
Crossing windows have coprime oriented gap factors, giving a simultaneous
product divisor on their common interior points. An actual ordered
example has complete cancellation of the two twist phases. These results
do not change the general growth bound. The descent extends to every
bipartition and preserves distinct points on its first step at `C=1/2`;
controlling the resulting separate clusters remains necessary. An
identical-column symmetry also reduces the ten-factor rational-solution
question to three explicit cubics and a square discriminant.
For a different ten-column `K5` code, exact rational polynomial reduction
excludes distinct absolute coefficients when two adjacent edges have
the prescribed ratio `1:2`. Item 408 now removes that ratio restriction
over the reals, using a complete order classification and exact positive
polynomial certificates. It concerns this moment model, not arbitrary
endpoint configurations.

Items 409--413 audit joint information after descent. Collision supports
give a fractional packing restriction and an explicit triple threshold.
A complementary four-row determinant has extra divisibility from mixed
selected and retained layers; that extra factor is absent on one-layer
prime profiles. A bounded matching residual reduces exactly to a bounded
rational-normal projection, while the associated split quadratic retains
the original tangent-half-angle coordinate. These statements give no new
unconditional growth estimate. Retaining its integer factors gives an
exact common divisor, but the resulting height gain is one on squarefree
allocation profiles. The needed simultaneous arithmetic gain
for arbitrary endpoint arcs remains unproved. The positive five-point
Ptolemy system now has an exact common primitive numerator factor, but
its extra gap-prime valuations are accidental chord contents and its
direct size bound is weaker than the existing triangle estimate.

Items 414--416 check proposed ways to use that positive content. The
exchange between adjacent pentagons cancels both forced gap powers from
its common primitive numerator. The gap powers retained in its denominator
come with a weaker size estimate. A projective-orbit audit gives an exact
least-radius functional only after normalizing against the transformed
anchor; its invariant content yields a lower bound for the orbit minimum,
where a new upper bound would be needed. Neither calculation improves
the general point-count growth rate. A separate combinatorial audit retains
the improved arc constant after every subset gcd is removed. Even with
that correction, nonnegative combinations of the existing five-row gap
and content estimates leave a factor greater than three in their radius
cost on the complete balanced profile. This conclusion is restricted to
those existing estimates, not a general obstruction to coupled methods.

Item 417 excludes the full signed six-factor representative family at
`C<=1/2`, even with moving rational coefficients. An exact ramified
valuation bound, combined with the existing odd-prime calculation and
polynomial chord identity, reaches this test constant and handles both
degenerate boundaries. This is a restricted-family exclusion: no
reduction of arbitrary endpoint configurations to that family is known,
and the general growth estimate remains unchanged.

Items 418--419 add two model theorems beyond that family. A parity
extension and the zero-edge boundary of the real `K5` certificates show
that five equal first-and-third moments need at least ten nonzero
distinct-magnitude factors. A separate differential divisor argument
bounds the number of polynomial rows by twelve, independently of degree,
when a constant rotation makes their common high-degree coefficients real.
Neither theorem supplies a reduction of arbitrary integer endpoint arcs
to its hypotheses. The uniform circle bound remains unproved.

Items 420--421 check two missing steps in these models. The natural
scalar differential construction fails on a primitive complex-jet
fixture, and rational common rotation followed by full polynomial gcd
removal restores the original tuple. The moment theorem, in contrast,
extends to repeated coefficients: five distinct aggregate integer rows
with equal first and third moments require total coordinate width at
least ten. Exact certificates exclude the new repeated-edge boundary.
This removes a fixed-factor restriction without improving the general
dependence on `R`.

Item 422 classifies the repeated six-factor first-moment case by an
exact finite enumeration. Its only two coefficient rays are signed
specializations of the already excluded representative. Combining this
with item 421 and the smaller-width distance bounds excludes five
persistent endpoint rows of effective width at most nine for fixed
rational factor constructions at `C<=1/2`. The factor width is bounded
in this theorem; arbitrary endpoint tuples remain outside its scope.

Item 423 proves endpoint-scale preservation for a family of nonconformal
maps on the four-point Pell source. Every fixed positive rational
alignment has a bounded image constant; one has exact constant below
fifteen, while a nearby moving alignment has unbounded width. Increasing
the radius or exceeding constant two does not invalidate this result.
It is a family calculation, without map existence for arbitrary tuples.

Item 424 gives exact ordinary contents for general endpoint swaps and
retains their full Gaussian denominator overlap. It also proves that
discarding target overlap cannot certify endpoint scale for five or
more points as the angular span shrinks. A successful map would need
large shared target denominators; existence of that sharing remains
unproved. This is an arithmetic requirement, not a new point-count bound.

Item 425 limits simultaneous preservation in this aligned family.
Along any shrinking-angle source family with at least five points, even
endpoint coordinate `x` and bounded normalized width, at most twelve
fixed positive integer alignments coprime to `x^2+1` can all have bounded
image widths. The number of source points may vary. This differs from
the four-point Pell family, but still leaves open a single successful
nonconformal alignment or an adaptive map.

Item 426 removes arbitrary enlargement of the cotangent clearing scale.
Each actual triangle half-determinant factors exactly into its Gaussian
content norm, three reduced cotangent denominators and a parity factor.
The resulting global identity retains conductor and residue contributions
together. Its height bound is the existing Vandermonde accounting in
intrinsic coordinates; it gives no new general growth rate.

Item 427 excludes a universal angular-order gain from nonzero fixed
linear combinations of triangle areas. Such combinations can still
cancel on special arithmetic shape loci. Anchored triangle Pluecker
relations also reduce to the already normalized positive Ptolemy system,
so that change of coordinates adds no new conductor saving.

Items 428--429 audit another use of endpoint symmetry. A relative map
parameter has an explicit height bound in terms of the two full primitive
radii, but this remains radius-dependent. Choosing a map to preserve a
four-point subset also fails on the actual five-point cubic family: all
three interior-pair choices have growing full target widths. Every fixed
positive rational nonconformal alignment fails on that family as well.
These results leave adaptive map existence for large, small-constant
tuples unresolved.

Item 430 controls varying rational alignments on that same five-point
family. Keeping a bounded full target width with a nonidentity parameter
`p/q` requires reduced height `p+q` at least a constant times `t^(2/5)`;
bounded `|p-q|` raises this to `t^(2/3)`. The exact Gaussian lcm argument
allows every parameter to vary, but supplies a necessary height cost,
not an exclusion of all adaptive maps.

Item 431 proves that full numerical invariant relations have full
rational image at every individual active cut. Their integral image
has cyclic quotient of an explicitly identified gcd ratio. Thus the
arithmetic proper-image restrictions concern short relations; full
rank alone cannot force their restrictions to vanish. These results
leave the general growth estimate unchanged.

Item 432 computes the complete Smith form of the integer squared-distance
matrix. For a primitive tuple its entry gcd is a square or twice a square,
according to coordinate parity; after removing it the last Smith factor
is `4Na^2` or `2Na^2`, with `N=R^2` and an explicit integer triangle
content `a`. This identity holds for actual points with arbitrary row
units. Its geometric estimate is still the known triangle bound, so it
does not establish the missing source-gcd inequality.

Item 433 adds a nonlinear condition on four short numerical relations
at an eight-row first-smaller cut. Their raw maximal minors satisfy a
Segre-cubic congruence, retaining prime powers and rank drops. Below
coefficient height `exp((1/6-o(1))w)` the congruence becomes an exact
cubic identity. The resulting point can be degenerate, and the existing
lattice estimate does not supply four relations this short at eight rows.

Item 434 extends this argument through a Chow form. At a fixed sufficiently
large row count, the existing lattice estimates do supply many relations
whose hyperplanes have a common point on the matching image at every
first-smaller cut. The image degree and every arithmetic content loss
are accounted for. The conclusion allows boundary points and zero
restriction images; it gives no contradiction or improved general growth.

Items 435--436 separate that geometric limitation from coefficient
height. A large actual numerical-zero space can have compatible boundary
points at every cut and no common polynomial factor. But its extension
induced by one fixed quartet cannot contribute a nonzero first-smaller
restriction at the required short height. An integral coefficient
extraction proves this even for sums of quartet relations and cancellation
against the deeper kernel. Reducing arbitrary short relations to such a
controlled subspace remains open.

Items 437--438 determine the conductor content, evaluation heights and
permutation-representation structure of every algebraic cut kernel.
The support proof works coefficient by coefficient and does not assume
graph spanning. The separate Gram-minor polarization proof identifies
the exact Specht constituents at each depth. These make the available
height comparisons precise, but do not turn proper restriction images
into the zero images needed for a uniform theorem.

Items 439--455 identify the coherent terminal kernels with conformal-block
annihilators and compute their determinant degrees and coalition content.
Weyl symmetry and a tensor-kernel argument give a stronger coefficient
divisibility bound. An explicit determinant construction proves that its
individual-prime multiplicity is sharp at every generic coalition. The
level-one determinant comparison reaches equality in every rank; the
other checked ranks and degrees still give no strict gain. Local fusion
flags do not yet provide a short vector in one global integer lattice.
These results leave the general growth estimate unchanged.

For configurations admitting a nonconformal rational projective map to
another endpoint configuration, items 300 and 302 now
prove the stronger **conditional** growth estimate
`M=O(sqrt(log R/loglog R))`. Existence of such a map for an arbitrary
configuration remains unproved; the general estimate above is unchanged.
The two fixed arc constants can be arbitrary, and no ordering of the
least radii is needed.

Items 341--342 now give a complete arithmetic search criterion for
such maps and prove that their possible source squared radii N<=X
form a set of size `O_epsilon(X^(247/496+epsilon))` when at least
128 points are retained and both endpoint constants are at most two.
This is a restriction on map-admitting norms, not an improved
unconditional point count or a proof that the required maps exist.

Item 305 gives a separate direct improvement, without an auxiliary map:
arcs containing an anchor of primitive radial length at most
`log R/loglog R` have `M=O_C(log R/(loglog R)^2)`. The existence of
such an anchor is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of the
short-arc condition.

Items 310--319 give new phase certificates for specified repeated Walsh
profiles, now with arbitrary distinct prime sizes, row units and common
Gaussian content. If all but `K` assigned labels follow a binary affine
map of corank at most `k`, then
`log R^2>=c_C M^2 log M/(2^k sqrt(M)+K)`.
Copy capacity also removes the rank parameter, giving
`log R^2>=c_C M^2 log M/(M^(3/4)+K)`.
Thus fixed corank and `K=O(sqrt(M))` give exponent `2/3`; arbitrary
rank and `K=O(M^(3/4))` give exponent `4/5`. Every fixed polynomially
sublinear exception allowance still gives an exponent below one.
Symplectic, ordinary-dot and canonical assignments are also covered by
their direct weighted proofs. These are restrictions on structured
profiles; no extraction theorem places arbitrary endpoint tuples in
these families.

Item 320 now removes every affinity and balance assumption from the
aligned-flat extraction in the repeated Walsh model. For arbitrary
nonlinear assignments and actual nearly equal prime logarithms, it gives
`M=O_C(1+log R (logloglog R)^2/(loglog R)^2)`.
This improves growth within that family. Items 333 and 335 now give a
growth improvement for every prime-weight assignment as well. Extending
the particular displayed rate to arbitrary weights remains open:
item 322 shows why one family chosen without reference to the weights
is insufficient, even after imposing every pair-phase inequality.
The best general circle bound above is unchanged.

Items 325--327 use the full collection of coset phase constraints.
For arbitrary nonlinear assignments and arbitrary prime sizes, they
force the total prime weight in the Walsh label classes to differ
from equal class weights by only `O_C(W0/log M)` in total variation.
This is an unconditional necessary condition within the repeated Walsh
model, not yet a growth improvement. An additional approximate-constant
pair-slack hypothesis outside at most `M^(1-delta)` directions does
give the same improved growth rate as item 320 for arbitrary prime
weights. Item 333 subsequently removes that extra hypothesis for a
qualitative improvement: all repeated-Walsh endpoint profiles satisfy
`W0/(M log M)->infinity`, and hence
`M=o_C(log R/loglog R)`. Quantitative vector-space Ramsey gives
`M=O_C(log R/[loglog R (log_2^* R)^(1/3)])`; item 335 sharpens this to
`M=O_C(log R log_2 T/[loglog R sqrt T])`, with `T=log_2^* R`.
The iterated logarithm counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one.
It uses four-row phase inequalities to bound
every pair-slack value, then applies finite-color vector-space Ramsey
and the nonlinear aligned-flat extraction. This is a family theorem;
arbitrary circle configurations have not been placed in this model.

For the backwards approach, a useful height-independent sufficient target
is: find one fixed integer `k` and `c_k>0` such that every `k` distinct
points on a circle of radius `R` span arc length at least `c_k sqrt(R)`.
Indeed, among `M>=k` ordered points in length `C sqrt(R)`, some consecutive
`k` span at most `(k-1)C sqrt(R)/(M-k+1)`: sum all consecutive-window
lengths and count each gap at most `k-1` times. The target would imply
`M<=k-1+(k-1)C/c_k`, uniformly in `R`. Conversely, failure of uniformity
produces, for every fixed `k`, clusters with normalized span tending to
zero. This is a reformulation of the missing problem, not a proved lower
bound; arguments must cover this regime regardless of how slowly `M`
diverges relative to `R`.

Item 132 gives a second exact formulation using an ordinary integer lcm
of all pair cotangent denominator norms. Its height inequality (H) is
equivalent to the uniform goal and is still unproved; see
[the integer lcm target](integer_cotangent_lcm_height_target.md).

## Verified progress

1. **All dependent pairs can be removed uniformly.** For sufficiently large
   `R`, any two multiplicatively dependent, distinct non-root ratios on a
   one-sided endpoint arc satisfy `u² = v` or `v² = u`. Their total incidence
   is bounded explicitly in terms of `C`. If `C < 1`, there are no such pairs.
   The proof works with arbitrary signed circle valuations, including prime
   powers; it does not require the entire grid to share one prime orientation.
   See [the proof and its formalization boundary](uniformity_continuation.md).

2. **An arbitrary-value balanced pattern is excluded.** In the complete
   seven-row, 35-column four-subset model, the eight circle points must span
   an arc of length at least `(4 / (3 sqrt(2))) R^(4/7)`. More generally,
   exactly balanced eight-point systems with total Gaussian unit one cannot
   occur in an arc of length `(1/2) sqrt(R)`. The proof uses nonzero integral
   projections onto the axes and diagonals, together with the product of
   complementary factors. It applies to arbitrary Gaussian block values,
   not only fixed polynomial templates. See
   [the phase proof, unit audit, and degenerate cases](phase_frontier_continuation.md).

3. **The missing extraction step is now explicit.** Restricting a larger
   balanced family to eight rows need not preserve balance. More generally,
   for a uniformly selected `2s`-row subset of `M` exactly balanced rows,
   the expected weighted defect is

   ```text
   s(M - 2s) W / (2(M - 1)).
   ```

   Complete equally weighted fair-cut systems attain this value for every
   subset, even when all point units agree. Unit pigeonholing therefore does
   not fix this obstruction. See
   [the independent audits and extraction calculation](multipoint_continuation.md).

4. **A sufficient finite arithmetic test is proved conditionally.** Appendix D
   of the same note shows exactly how an improvement in an eight-point local
   inequality would imply the uniform bound. The averaging error for a
   symmetric test is at most `42 osc(f) W / M`, with all prime-power and
   common-factor normalizations tracked. The needed local improvement is
   explicitly left unproved.

5. **The complete primitive chord residue is explicit.** For eight points
   in one Gaussian-unit class, let `T` be the product of the 28 positive
   primitive imaginary parts. With the exact angular-gap slack `S_arc`,

   ```text
   D + 2 log T + 2 S_arc = 2 W + 56 log(C / 2).
   ```

   If every conductor layer is balanced and some valuation row has no
   complementary row, then `T >= R^(1/14) / 100`, without any initial
   short-arc assumption. The proof combines a connected graph of large
   valuation distances with the rational-ray theorem. This includes the
   complete 35-profile model. See
   [the exact residue identity and power-growth proof](balanced_bonus_phase_audit.md).

6. **Cyclic order gives an additional arithmetic inequality.** Ordered
   Ptolemy identities imply

   ```text
   L - 3 A <= 12 log T - 140 log 2,
   ```

   where `L` counts weighted two-versus-two quadruples and `A` counts their
   alternating patterns. This supplies a conductor-scale residue gain when
   alternating patterns are absent. Such interval-cut endpoint clusters
   already admit a simpler bound of three points at `C = 1/2`. Symmetric
   critical cut distributions have `L - 3 A = 0`, so the new inequality does
   not resolve their case. See
   [the prime-power identity, counting proof, and limitation](ordered_residue_growth.md).

7. **A growing range of radial directions is controlled.** Suppose the
   arc contains a lattice point `P = (x,y)` with primitive radial length
   `R / gcd(|x|,|y|) <= A (log R)^sigma`, for fixed `A > 0` and
   `0 < sigma < 1/2`. For sufficiently large `R`, the arc has at most five
   points, or three if `P` is an endpoint. Integral rotation reduces this
   to three simultaneous square offsets; Bugeaud's effective two-Pell
   theorem excludes them with all coefficient dependence retained. See
   [the exact chord parametrization and growing-height slice](endpoint_independent_attack.md).
   The [independent audit](endpoint_radial_slice_audit.md) also extends the
   permitted radial length to
   `A sqrt(log R) / (log log R)^(3/2)` for
   `0 < A < 1 / (C^2 sqrt(K))`, where `K` is the absolute constant in
   Bugeaud's theorem.

8. **The four-point shortcut is false, even with canonical units.** An
   explicit primitive Pell family has four equal canonical Gaussian units,
   fixed primitive chord residues, private-layer weight `V_1 = log 5`, and
   balanced-layer weight `V_2 = W - log 5` tending to infinity. Its arc
   length divided by `sqrt(R)` tends to zero. Thus no positive coefficient
   can force `2 log T >= delta V_2 - O(1)` for every four-point endpoint
   cluster. A single bounded private factor can invalidate a direct
   extension of the exact-balanced phase argument. See
   [the canonical-primary counterexample and complete proof](canonical_four_point_counterexample.md)
   and [a smaller-residue variant with `T = 48`](four_point_bonus_counterexample.md).
   These are four-point examples, not counterexamples to uniform boundedness.

9. **Fixed shifted-Pell templates have a uniform count.** For any real
   quadratic algebraic-integer unit, products of fixed shifted Pell blocks
   with fixed multiplicities and fixed Gaussian prefactors can have at most
   **eight** distinct primitive endpoint points along unbounded indices.
   Their total active exponent width is at most `12`, and seven or more
   rows force that width to be at most four. The proof establishes
   bounded common-factor loss and compares phase cancellation with the
   coefficient mass required by conjugate polynomial roots. The smallest
   quadratic unit requires an additional exact argument: shortest
   polynomial differences form an integer-grid graph, whose edge count
   rules out seven rows in the remaining width-twelve case. These bounds
   are independent of the field and fixed template, but the index
   at which the asymptotic argument applies is not uniform. See
   [the quadratic-unit theorem and exact hypotheses](quadratic_unit_template_bound.md).
   Eight rows force a full four-factor parity class for every unit, and
   their intrinsic statistics satisfy `D = O(1)` and `W_4 = W - O(1)`,
   with fixed-template constants and no disjoint-support assumption.
   For the canonical unit `9 + 4 sqrt(5)`, the active width is at most
   four even for two rows. See also
   [the earlier direct proof and nonresonant-rate extension](pell_product_endpoint_obstruction.md).

10. **A second Pell classification allows more general coefficients.**
    For at most seven pairwise norm-coprime, conjugate-coprime Pell blocks
    over `Q(sqrt(5))` whose leading coefficients share a complex ray,
    eight persistent endpoint rows again force exactly four blocks and
    their full parity class. In the quadratic phase case, eight rows are
    also excluded in degrees five through ten. The proof uses leading
    phases and exact sums of distinct norm-one coefficients. For a fixed
    private conductor of norm `N_0`, disjoint from the growing blocks,
    the resulting eight-row family satisfies
    `D + W_4 <= 2 W + 14 log N_0`. See
    [the shared-ray classification and its limitations](pell_shared_ray_classification.md).

11. **Higher phase moments give exact separation bounds.** If two
    same-parity sign rows have equal odd moments `1,3,...,2a-1` in
    distinct positive quadratic norm-one coefficients, then their Hamming
    distance is at least `4a+2`. Unequal subset sizes are allowed. The
    proof compares the lowest and highest odd coefficients of a product
    polynomial; equality forces a single central odd monomial. Combined
    with endpoint phase expansions, this proves further specified degree
    ranges of the shared-ray conductor bonus. The resulting estimates
    still have fixed-family constants. See
    [the exact moment lemma, sharpness example, and degree table](odd_moment_separation.md).

12. **The first orthogonal twelve-factor pattern is excluded.** No
    eight-by-twelve sign matrix with orthogonal rows admits a positive
    vector of distinct entries for which both the vector and its
    coordinatewise reciprocal have equal row sums. A rank-four Gram
    complement and root-system classification reduce the proof to
    repeated-column collisions. This excludes every distance-six
    equality code in the twelve-factor shared-ray moment problem,
    without assuming that the rows extend to a Hadamard matrix. It does
    not cover all nonorthogonal codes. See
    [the completion-free proof and remaining scope](critical_pell_moment_codes.md).
    A further exact four-term row identity excludes all 4,096 column
    signings of the explicit nonorthogonal critical pattern in that note.
    Its proof allows signed nonzero coefficients and forces repeated
    absolute values; it does not assume positivity after column changes.

13. **The four-coordinate identity has a finite sector version.** For the
    explicit nonorthogonal twelve-factor pattern, suppose its four selected
    Gaussian factors occupy a sector of width less than `pi/12`, the
    prefactor phase cancels as specified, and their signed product is
    nonreal. An arc of angular width `Delta < pi/4` then satisfies
    `Delta >= 3/(2P)`, where `P` is the product of those four moduli.
    At endpoint scale this forces their log norm to be at least half
    `W`, plus `2 log(3/(2C))`. This is a finite inequality allowing
    factors to vary with the radius. The sector, phase, and extraction
    hypotheses remain unresolved for arbitrary configurations. See
    [the finite proof and stable reciprocal identity](finite_sector_certificate.md).
    Without a sector restriction, the same identity gives the weaker
    finite bound `Delta >= 3/(8P^2)`, forcing selected weight at least
    `W/4 + log(3/(8C))`. The prefactor-phase and pattern hypotheses
    are still required.

14. **All integer combinations give a finite bound, but not a complete
    route.** For a zero-sum integer coefficient vector `c` with nonzero
    combined valuations, let `H(c)` be the weighted absolute combined
    prime exponents. Its Gaussian imaginary residue `t_c >= 1` satisfies
    `H(c) >= W/2 + 2 log(4 t_c/(C ||c||_1))`. This includes arbitrary
    prime powers. A countable-union argument constructs formal balanced
    factor systems with arbitrarily many real-circle points that satisfy
    every such imaginary-part lower bound simultaneously, with compatible
    actual phases. The factors and residues are not asserted to be
    Gaussian integers. Thus these separation bounds alone still omit
    essential arithmetic. See
    [the finite inequality and the all-combinations relaxation](integer_combination_separation.md).

15. **Direct balanced pair products expose the missing phase branches.**
    For every even exactly balanced common-unit cluster, complementary
    rows force `C >= 2`. Without complementary rows, the finite rational-ray
    product argument excludes the axis/diagonal mean-direction branches
    at `C = 1/2`; all branches are rational when there are eight rows.
    In the complete equal-weight half-cut model, every integral monomial
    in the linear row-phase space is classified, and the only nonzero
    ones of log norm at most `W/2` are these pair products. Their height
    is `(M-2) W/(2(M-1))`. Thus another small monomial in that space does
    not repair the irrational-branch gap. See
    [the finite pair-product proof and exact height classification](balanced_pair_products.md).

16. **Exact pair-product collisions have a sharp endpoint obstruction.**
    Four nonzero Gaussian integers of radius `R` satisfying a nontrivial
    relation `z0 z3 = z1 z2`, on an arc of angular width less than `pi`,
    force arc length at least `2 sqrt(2) sqrt(R)`. Gaussian gcd
    factorization and the even integral squared distance between
    equal-norm factors prove the bound; a three-point family approaches
    equality. Thus a `C=1/2` cluster has exactly `M(M+1)/2` distinct
    unordered pair products and ordered multiplicative energy `2M^2-M`.
    Combined with item 9, this improves the fixed quadratic-unit template
    count to six whenever `C < 2 sqrt(2)`: seven rows would force two
    complementary exponent pairs, whose fixed prefactors cancel by the
    shrinking-angle limit.
    This does not bound the size of a collision-free cluster. See
    [the proof, sharpness family, and counting limitation](multiplicative_rectangle_separation.md).
    This result is a prose proof, not a Lean theorem.

17. **Higher product collisions are excluded for arbitrary configurations.**
    At `C=1/2`, equality of two products of up to eight arc points,
    allowing repetitions, forces equality of the multisets. The bound
    extends through nine factors when `R>=1024`. More generally,
    `C<=1/(2k)` guarantees this rigidity through any fixed length `k`.
    Equal-radius reflection identities for polynomial coefficients,
    derivative bounds near the arc midpoint, and Gaussian integrality
    prove these finite statements. No prime-pattern or template
    hypothesis is used. Distinct product counts alone still give no
    uniform cardinality bound, since the product arcs have a larger
    radius exponent. See
    [the coefficient estimate, exact constants, and scope](short_arc_product_rigidity.md).
    These are prose proofs with exact rational checks of the constants.

18. **Angular moment cancellation strengthens product rigidity.**
    The radius-independent condition `k C^2 <= 8` makes every endpoint
    arc a multiplicative `B_k` set. In particular, `C=1/2` now gives
    rigidity through thirty-two factors. Equal argument means improve
    the first Gaussian-sum bound to `k R Delta^2/8`; an exact integral
    with frequencies `-(r-1),...,r` then bounds successive coefficient
    differences by `(k/r)(C^2/4)^r`. Gaussian integrality finishes the
    induction. If angular unwrapping fails, the same hypothesis makes
    the arc shorter than the distance between two equal-norm lattice
    points. See [the proof and remaining counting gap](angular_moment_product_rigidity.md).
    This is a prose proof with exact checks of the cancellation identities.

19. **Short integer circuits improve the width-four family count.**
    Any affine dependence among distinct integer vectors in a box of
    total width at most four has a relation with at most ten terms on
    each side, counted with multiplicity. For a persistent fixed-exponent
    Gaussian factor family, shrinking angles make the corresponding
    fixed prefactors cancel exactly. Product rigidity then limits such
    families to five rows whenever `10 C^2<=8`. This improves the
    quadratic-unit count at `C=1/2` for every `lambda>sqrt(11)`, including
    `9+4 sqrt(5)`. The argument does not require a Pell recurrence but
    does require fixed exponents, fixed prefactors, and width at most
    four. See [the circuit proof and scope](small_width_affine_circuits.md).
    A finite extension now removes persistence: with common prefactor
    modulus at most `H`, the same five-point bound holds when
    `R>50 C^2 H^20`. For Gaussian-unit prefactors it holds at every
    radius, with arbitrary Gaussian block values, overlaps, and common
    factors. Total active width at most four is still essential to
    this argument.

20. **The relation route does not exclude the full balanced patterns.**
    The complete half-cut incidence matrix has strictly positive Gram
    form on the zero-sum subspace: its value is
    `B M/(4(M-1)) ||c||^2`. All row subsets therefore remain affinely
    independent after their own common-factor normalization. Combined
    with the all-combinations imaginary-part bounds, this excludes
    product collisions of every length in the short-phase relaxation.
    Full exponent rank alone would not suffice for arbitrary complex
    factors. Distinct split Gaussian primes also realize these
    patterns as arbitrarily large primitive multiplicatively independent
    lattice configurations, without a short-arc assertion. Thus the
    recent rigidity theorems still leave the simultaneous Gaussian
    factor/phase restriction unresolved. See
    [the exact rank calculation and scope audit](relation_free_balanced_patterns.md).
    Section 7 of the [finite-test note](finite_local_test_attack.md)
    now checks the intrinsic target explicitly: at 64 rows its excess
    after normalization is `(29/8507) W'`, while compatible short
    phases, all integer-combination separation bounds, every subset
    determinant bound, and all product-rigidity conclusions coexist.
    The factors are still not Gaussian integers. This isolates the
    missing arithmetic more precisely; it is not a lattice counterexample.
    Sections 4.1--4.2 of the
    [all-combinations note](integer_combination_separation.md) now prove
    that its canonical equal-modulus factors cannot all be Gaussian
    integers, even after a common rotation. Any Gaussian realization
    in the same zero-winding phase branch would need kernel-phase
    oscillation at least
    `sqrt(2) exp(-W/(2B)) - (M-1)Delta/B`, much larger than the point
    phase width for fixed `M` and growing `W`. Other kernel components,
    winding lifts, and unequal moduli remain uncontrolled.
    Section 4.3 further excludes independent rotations of every
    complementary factor pair. Only the complement-antisymmetric
    kernel component can repair this particular obstruction; its
    dimension is `B/2-M+1`. This residual dimension grows with `M`,
    so the refinement does not give a uniform count.

21. **Working backward gives a sharper unconditional sublogarithmic proof.**
    Let `Y=max_(p^e || R^2) p^ceil(e/2)`. A single Gaussian divisor
    of norm at least `Y` divides at least half the points; the entire
    prime power is selected before pigeonholing. Also
    `log R <= psi(Y) <= (log 4+4)Y`. Combining these facts with the
    existing Ramana obstruction yields
    `M <= (4+epsilon) log R/log(log R)` for fixed `C,epsilon>0`
    and sufficiently large radius. An explicit finite bound and all
    split, inert, and ramified cases are given in
    [the inverse-descent note](inverse_prime_power_descent.md).
    This is a complete prose derivation; its prime-power assembly is
    not yet Lean-verified. The existing Lean theorem still has constant
    `8+epsilon`. The same note proves a finite uniform count when
    all points have one Gaussian square class up to units, and identifies
    parity agreement as an inverse question. It does not prove
    that arbitrary clusters satisfy that hypothesis.

22. **Backward descent now controls full valuation profiles and near-extremizers.**
    A divisor of norm `D` retaining `k` points satisfies
    `k log D <= 2 log R+4k max(0,log C)`, including `k=1,2`.
    With `X=exp(2 log R/M+4 max(0,log C))`, each prime power
    `p^e || R^2` consequently satisfies
    `p^m_e <= X`, where `m_e=floor((e+1)^2/4)/(e+1)` is the
    optimal single-prime interval-profile constant. This gives
    `log N_rep <= 4 X^(3/2) log X` for the repeated-prime-power
    part of the norm, and improves the leading constant to
    `3+epsilon` when the norm is squarefull. A sequence approaching
    constant four must put all but `o(log R)` norm weight into
    exponent-one split primes of size `(log R)^(1+o(1))`.
    Their cuts are almost balanced and pairwise almost independent;
    about `M/2` such prime columns remain. This clarifies why parity
    agreement is not automatic: distinct nonassociate points of a
    squarefree norm have different Gaussian valuation parities.
    See [the valuation-profile proof](inverse_valuation_profile.md).
    These are prose results. They neither prove uniformity nor
    classify unbounded clusters growing below the sublogarithmic scale.

23. **A radius-independent extraction handles every unbounded growth regime.**
    For common-unit endpoint clusters with `C<=2`, the weighted prime-layer
    sign vectors are unit vectors with pairwise nonpositive inner products.
    Their Bessel bound is `sum_i <f_i,h>^2<=2||h||^2`. It implies that, for
    any fixed `k,eta>0`, a cluster with
    `M>=k-1+2(2^k-1)^2/eta^2` contains `k` points whose inherited cut
    patterns all have weight within relative error `eta` of `2^(-k)W`.
    For `k=8`, intrinsic normalization gives weights approaching `W'/127`
    on every nontrivial unoriented cut. The limiting excess in the
    sufficient arithmetic target is `(D+W_4-2W')/W'=21/127>0`.
    Thus it suffices to exclude a fixed neighborhood of this profile;
    the selected normalized radius also tends to infinity. This applies
    even when the original cardinalities grow arbitrarily slowly in `R`.
    The exclusion itself remains unproved. See
    [the extraction, finite constants, and precise missing theorem](uniform_profile_extraction.md).
    The Hilbert-space Bessel ingredient is checked in
    [ObtuseBessel.lean](../GaussianChain/ObtuseBessel.lean); the complete
    extraction and Gaussian application remain prose proofs.
    The larger-tuple version shows that a local gain
    `D+delta W_(k/2)<=(k/4)W+B` suffices whenever
    `delta binom(k,k/2)>k(k-1)/2`. Thus even `delta=10^(-6)` would
    suffice on a fixed 32-point tuple. The gain itself is still missing;
    this is a uniformity-oriented reduction, not a new growth-rate bound.

The earlier [multipoint note](multipoint_continuation.md) also proves a
rational-normal incidence estimate and gives an explicit four-point family
disproving bounded adjacent-chord recurrence coefficients, even when
consecutive primitive chord determinants equal one.

24. **Rational projective symmetry gives a bounded-radius theorem for
    fixed configurations.** For every fixed rational configuration of
    at least five distinct directions, all of its rational projective
    images realized as lattice points in endpoint arcs have bounded
    radius. The proof permits arbitrary common rational Gaussian
    multipliers: the exact minimum radius for directions
    `epsilon_j d_j/conjugate(d_j)` is
    `|lcm(d_j)|/|gcd(d_j)|`. After normalizing the two Gaussian matrix
    columns, pair gcds and the product of the individual coordinate
    contents control the denominator cost. For five points whose two
    normalized cross-ratio heights are at most `B`, an explicit
    consequence is `R <= 2^56 C^10 B^96`. Four points have the lower
    normalized-span bound `1/(16 B^(9/2))`; a fixed four-point template
    can nevertheless persist at large radius. The constants depend on
    the rational template, and none of this gives uniform cardinality.
    The proof and a separate audit are in
    [the projective note](fresh_algebraic_parallel.md) and Section 6 of
    [the independent audit](uniformity_audit_parallel.md).

25. **The extracted cross-ratios necessarily have growing heights.**
    For arbitrary prime exponents, exact cancellation of four primitive
    chord formulas gives a rational cross-ratio whose conductor
    numerator and denominator cannot be canceled by their opposing
    residues. An inherited relative-`eta` uniform profile therefore
    forces every ordered cross-ratio `x` to satisfy
    `R^((1-eta)/4) <= H(x) <= (C^2/4) R^((1+5eta)/4)`.
    Thus these invariants have height `R^(1/4+o(1))`, which is compatible
    with item 24. Real compactness cannot supply bounded rational
    height: an explicit family with all real cross-ratios convergent
    has all rational cross-ratio heights tending to infinity. A
    bounded-height quadruple extraction from large endpoint clusters
    would itself imply the sought uniform theorem. See Section 7 of
    [the audit](uniformity_audit_parallel.md) and
    [the extraction obstruction](projective_height_extraction_obstruction.md).

26. **The entire reflection group can fail to generate another integral
    point.** For arbitrarily large actual Gaussian configurations with
    complete balanced cut patterns, the group generated by all anchor
    pair reflections has integral orbit exactly the original points.
    This includes words with nonintegral intermediate points. For
    nearly equal cut weights, every new orbit point has denominator
    modulus at least `R^((1-eta)m/(4(m-1)))`. These configurations are
    not asserted to occupy endpoint arcs. The result rules out a
    proposed unrestricted reflection-orbit descent mechanism, without
    disproving uniformity. See
    [the full-orbit calculation](symmetry_descent_parallel.md).

27. **Generic polynomial divisibility has an exact endpoint exponent
    ceiling.** For a nonzero row-multihomogeneous polynomial `F` of
    total degree `D`, let `v` be its Taylor order at the anchored
    short-phase point. If `nu_S^+` and `nu_S^-` are its generic
    vanishing orders along the two isotropic directions on the rows
    in `S`, then
    `2^(-m) sum_S(nu_S^+ + nu_S^-) <= (D-v)/2`.
    Reciprocity reduces this to the multiplicity Schwartz--Zippel
    inequality on a two-point grid. In the uniform half-angle block
    model this bounds the prescribed-divisor exponent by exactly the
    archimedean exponent `(D-v)/2`. Products of brackets and norm
    polynomials attain equality. Hence these generic orders and this
    Taylor estimate cannot supply a fixed positive power saving in
    the radius, even for forms beyond the bracket algebra. The proof
    does not control additional arithmetic divisibility, special-value
    cancellation, or unrestricted changing coefficients and degrees.
    See [the general polynomial theorem](hermitian_polynomial_barrier.md)
    and [its bracket precursor](plucker_compatibility_route.md).
    The latter also constructs exact Gaussian-compatible CRT data
    satisfying all prescribed cut valuations and Pluecker identities;
    their large residues explicitly fail the required endpoint bounds.

28. **Projective inverse-sieve normalization has a substantial
    conductor cost.** For squarefree circle norm `N`, the radial
    directions reduce to two isotropic classes at each `p|N`.
    Sending three radial anchors to `0,1,infinity` makes every
    conductor prime bad: `N` divides the determinant of the primitive
    integer transformation. The radial coordinate is different from
    the rational half-angle parameter. A separate finite projective
    interpolation theorem gives the exact coefficient-lattice index
    `Q^(r(r+1))` for two classes of multiplicity `r`. Even allowing
    arbitrary multiplicities depending on each prime and full cut
    yields no improvement over the pair-determinant threshold in the
    uniform profile. This abstract fourth-root calculation is not an
    endpoint reduction: natural radial height is `R=N^(1/2)`, and
    small coefficient powers of `X^2+Y^2` merely evaluate to `N^r`.
    See [the inverse-sieve audit](projective_inverse_sieve_route.md).

29. **Several short Gaussian relations reproduce the residue barrier.**
    For the integer matrix with columns `(Re B_i,Im B_i)`, the
    saturated relation lattice has covolume
    `sqrt(sum D_ij^2)/gcd(D_ij)`. Every minor of several short relations
    inherits explicit private-factor divisibility from the complementary
    column supports; maximal minors are exactly the complementary
    original pair minors divided by their gcd. The resulting
    successive-minima and divisibility constraints admit a common
    feasible exponent assignment. In the independent-block uniform
    model, with the intrinsic improvement of the arc width retained,
    maximal minors have zero leading margin and smaller minors have
    slack. Thus this checks the multiple-short-relations possibility
    without incorrectly dismissing exact linear relations. The block
    calculation is not asserted for arbitrary nested prime-power
    layers. See [the dual-lattice argument](auxiliary_form_route.md).

Items 24--29 are prose results, independently checked where indicated;
they add no formal endpoint theorem. That parallel research round did
not improve the general growth bound from item 21. The subsequent
residue investigation gives the following additional results.

30. **Inert-prime residue collisions handle all units without a
    pigeonhole loss.** Divide by the actual common Gaussian gcd,
    so no prime `p=3 mod 4` divides the remaining norm. For every
    pair put `c_ij=(z_i-z_j)/gcd_G(z_i,z_j)`, without restricting
    point units. The cut bound gives
    `log product|c_ij| <= b_M log R+binom(M,2)log C`, where
    `b_M=M/4` for even `M` and `(M-1)/4` for odd `M`.
    At every inert prime-power depth, the norm conic has
    `(p+1)p^(a-1)` residue classes; equal classes force the same
    rational prime power to divide `c_ij`. Balanced occupancy gives
    an exact finite function `F(M)` bounding the cofactor product
    below. The weighted Mertens theorem in `3 mod 4` implies
    `F(M)>=(1/4+o(1))M^2 log M`, hence the improved general
    prose estimate `M <= (1+epsilon)log R/log log R`.
    This is an incidental leading-constant improvement, not a
    growth-rate improvement or a uniformity proof. The finite
    inequality, analytic input and two independent audits are in
    [the inert-prime cofactor proof](inert_prime_cofactor_bound.md).

31. **Primitive residue content has an exact hierarchy.** In one
    common-unit class, for every subset `I` of primitive half-angle
    rows, the gcd of their real two-by-two minors equals
    `N(gcd_G(h_i:i in I)) gcd(t_ij:i<j in I)`.
    After removing that Gaussian gcd, the subset's Smith invariants
    are `(1,gcd t_ij)`. Moreover `gcd(t_ai,t_aj)` divides `t_ij`,
    so residue valuations are ultrametric at every prime, including
    conductor primes. This is genuine additional integer structure.
    It does not give inexpensive geometric descent: an explicit
    four-point endpoint family has fixed `T=768` and content two,
    but the natural fixed map `(X,Y)->(X,Y/2)` raises its least
    radius from order `t^4` to order `t^6` and destroys endpoint
    scale. See [the content theorem and exact cost example](residue_content_descent.md).

32. **Full profiles force large coefficients in several classes of
    polynomial relations.** Anchor a `k`-point inherited relative-`eta` uniform
    profile and let `A_1,...,A_(k-1)` be its primitive Gaussian
    half-angle factors. Every nonzero Gaussian-integer relation
    `c_0+sum c_j A_j=0` satisfies
    `max_j log max(1,|c_j|)>=(1-eta)W/2^k`.
    Common and private gcds supplied by the reference-isolated and
    reference-plus-one-isolated threshold patterns prove this for
    arbitrary prime powers. Consequently `1,A_1,...,A_(k-1)` are
    linearly independent over the field of negligible-height
    sequences, while their imaginary parts belong to that field.
    This supplies a nondegeneracy input for the moving-coefficient
    viewpoint. It does not bound the primitive residues: known
    reconstruction relations contain large conductor coefficients.
    The argument extends to every binary-box polynomial with fixed
    positive exponent steps, and to every homogeneous quadratic
    relation. These statements allow arbitrary prime powers.
    The cited moving-target theorems still require a fixed prime
    support. An explicit moving-support example has arbitrarily
    prescribed finite-degree nondegeneracy and a gcd whose logarithm
    is proportional to the height, disproving removal of that
    hypothesis even with the new independence input. Nor is a sum of a cut block's prime valuations
    itself a valuation. See [the moving-residue field analysis](moving_residue_field_route.md).

33. **Local residue congruences can be separated from the global
    height problem.** Outside the conductor, residue valuations are
    exact congruence depths on norm conics, with nested partitions
    of bounded local branching. Genuine Gaussian families with
    arbitrary fixed cardinality have bounded primitive residues and
    unbounded radius, so residue size alone does not control radius;
    their singleton conductor profiles and growing normalized arcs
    explicitly fail the large uniform-profile endpoint hypotheses.
    At conductor primes, collisions occur only within equal-allocation
    groups and follow unit-torus residue trees. Every permitted local
    tree can be realized locally; these branching constraints alone
    therefore supply no extra global height theorem. A bounded
    residue valuation also cannot bound the entire conductor power
    over a prime dividing that residue.
    The exact local analysis is in
    [the residue-prime investigation](residue_prime_incidence.md).

34. **Arbitrary prime allocations can be rounded with negligible-height
    errors on almost all rows.** For `W=log R^2`, put
    `E_i=sum_p min(a_ip,e_p-a_ip)log p`. Endpoint pair distances and
    a coarea identity prove `sum_i E_i<=W sqrt(M)/2`. Rounding each
    allocation to its nearer endpoint therefore changes almost all
    rows by rational rotations of logarithmic Weil height `o(W)`.
    It preserves the uniform profile of any fixed extracted tuple.
    The rounded prime powers form independent Gaussian blocks of
    equal asymptotic weight. The original short arc gives exact
    equations `q_i X_i+p_i Y_i=t_i!=0` on their row products, with
    all coefficients and values of logarithmic height `o(W)`.
    Rounded points need not stay on a short arc. See
    [the rounding theorem and moving equations](endpoint_allocation_rounding.md).

35. **The polynomial comparison persists for these moving equations.**
    After restoring the original small imaginary parts with the
    Gaussian twists, any bounded-degree polynomial with moving
    negligible-height coefficients has generic conductor-divisor
    exponent at most its usual archimedean exponent. The proof uses
    the multiplicity grid inequality with moving centers and also
    controls coefficient-prime divisibility. It covers inhomogeneous
    and Gram/conjugation expressions, while leaving special-value
    cancellation and conductor-sized coefficients outside its scope.
    See [the moving polynomial comparison](twisted_auxiliary_polynomial_barrier.md).

36. **Central truncation gives exact integral factors and permits a
    growing extracted tuple.** For every fixed `0<c<1/2`, an
    unbounded sequence of `M`-point clusters supplies
    `k=floor(c log_2 M)` rows with exact factorizations
    `z_i=B_i z_i^core`. All `B_i` are Gaussian integers of the same
    modulus `D`, with `log D<=kW/sqrt(M)`. Removing the outermost
    threshold layers leaves independent Gaussian blocks, each with
    its full asymptotic relative weight. Simultaneously controlling
    pair Fourier moments gives primitive half-angle numerators
    `h_i=K_i A'_i`, where `A'_i` is the core row product. Both the
    coefficient height `log|K_i|` and the height of the nonzero
    integer `Im(h_i)` are `o(log N(H'_S))` for every individual
    core block `H'_S`, even as their number grows. This is stronger
    than merely being `o(W)`. The original angular scale is retained;
    no short-arc property of the core points is asserted. See
    [the exact truncation and simultaneous extraction](endpoint_central_truncation.md).

37. **An explicit denominator budget rules out an unfaithful
    function-field transfer.** A rational-function model with
    arbitrarily many rows satisfies every infinity-scale product
    identity and has constant imaginary row values. But the
